Anyway, it's a long debated issue that basically revolves around
card-rarity versus
game-mechanics. VTES in itself is not constructed for card-limits, which
of course
should be no hindrance for your playgroup to have whatever house-rules
you
feel happy with. I for one was introduced to this game in a group who
did have
a card-limit house-rule. However, after a while certain parts of the
game started
to seem very strange, so we looked up the actual rules and learned that
there
wasn't supposed to be any card-limits.

One very often used argument against card-limit rules is based on the
example
of a stealth-bleed deck hunting for example a dominate/presence
vote-deck.
I think you can find the numerous bleed-modifiers you could place four
each
of in the bleed-deck. For the voter the limit would be eight cards in
total.

Another example is your generic potence combat-deck that would be
limited to
four Immortal Grapple and four Psyche to counter Majesty, Catatonic Fear

and Staredown.

There are certain strategies which simply become impossible with a
card-limit.
Just try playing some of the cards meant for the Setites and you'll see
what happens.

With a card-limit you'll change the balance of the game. It may work out
fine
for you, but I feel that it's not only a card-limit but also a
game-limit. When
you encounter a deck with a sick amount of the same card it'll usually
be a rather
common card, and what's more important, the deck will probably don't
function
very well. Another problem with card-limits within the scope of
card-rarity is
that strictly mathematically you'll get more of some unusual cards and
less of
some. Let's assume you own five Majesty and three Catatonic Fear and you

feel that you really need exactly eight combat-ends cards - well there
you are.

mostly harmless wrote:
> Now I would be interested to hear from people who played with and without

> Does playing without CL result in less creative deck building or in oder
> words: do decks that are build around many copies of just a few cards get

Those two ideas are not the same.

Many copies of the same few cards != less creative.

The NL (no limit) side would argue that 4CL forces a homogenized environment
(every combat deck packs 4 Bum's Rushes, 4 Ambushes, etc.), which they (the
NL side) would consider "less creative". Finding the proper ratios of cards
vs. simply putting 4 copies of each useful (or nearly useful) card.

But no matter - whatever your group enjoys.

> Another reason for us keeping the CL is that it would seem that NCL gives
> players with more cards an unfair advantage. Sure there are quite a lot of
> good common cars, but there are some powerful rare cards (like e.g. Shotgun
> Ritual or Freak Drive) that players with a lower budget have a hard time
> obtaining in higher quantity.

The NL side would say that 4CL gives players with more cards an unfair
advantage. The cards are designed so that the commons are the most widely
useful - the player with few cards who has 12 Majesties but only 1 Catatonic
Fear can only play 5 of those, as opposed to Mr. Suitcase who can play
with 4 of each. Many more examples of this exist (where a rare can be
substituted for a closely-related common).

> So my second question would be: Aren't there quite some rare cards that when
> used without CL can give a deck a great advantage?

A well-built NL deck will have some advantages over a CL deck, sure: it
can use the "best" cards for its plan in the "best" ratios (without having
to dilute them with close-but-no-cigar variations on the cards). The
cards are designed to be balanced in this NL environment - adding an
additional restriction to the deck (CL) will naturally add a disadvantage
to the deck - that's the nature of restrictions.

A deck can be built around many copies of a card (rare or not), yes.
This doesn't give that deck a "great advantage" over all other decks
(unless all other decks are somehow restricted to 4CL).

True, but a single WwEF or Forced Awakening works fine. If the initial block
was taken by a minion that was made available by such a play, then the blocker
need only increase his intercept to match the new stealth and block again.
And there's also all the usual prevention for S:CE. Form of Mist is a good
card but hardly a guarantee of victory. And protean is a discipline which is
seldom found in minions which can benefit greatly from the stealth and combat-
avoidance.

> Or a stealth deck with a large amount of Minion Taps and 5th Traditions for
> supreme blood support.

Minion Taps are commons. Fifth Traditions are nasty, albeit limited to Princes.

> It makes me wonder if not at least *some* cards should be limited.

Limiting, as with restricted cards in Magic, is basically an admission that you
have a problem with a card. To the extent that it reduces one's ability to
rely on powerful combos, it may be a reasonable concept. To limit a card which
is overpowered in and of itself, it's a self-contradiction which reduces the
game to luck of the draw of "good cards". Not that luck of the draw isn't a
factor anyway, I'd prefer not to make the situation any worse. Unless the
game is truly being dominated by the effects of a card (and I suppose Fifth
Tradition is probably as close a card as any in the game, for what it's
worth), I think it's better to allow all players to use the card as much as they
want. And if they get handjammed with the card, they have only themselves to
blame.

Boring to play against is a completely subjective statement--what is boring to
you is probably a good game to me. Thus, you can't really look as "boring" as
an objective result of playing the game by the rules.

I play in a pretty solid playgroup that really likes to push the game, and
makes lots of different decks all the time. When I make my decks, they are
generally pretty focused--my most obvious example is my Rush deck that does
nothing but Bum's Rush and kill opposing vampires. Every action. It doesn't
block. It has no intercept. No votes. No untap. Limited pool gain. Just lots
and lots of killing. Every action I take is generally a Bum's Rush followed by
the torporization of some vampire, until it becomes a good idea to bleed
someone.

Might this be considered "boring" by someone? Probably, but so what? It wins
sometimes, it looses sometimes. Where the interest comes for me is in the
strategic interaction between decks. I don't play VTES to see lots of different
cards (I've seen them all already) or funny card combos (while I certainly
appreciate them, they are generally too tenuous to actually play around). I
play to see how deck strategy "A" does against deck strategy "B". How does my
Rush deck do against a Stealth and Bleed deck? How about a weenie Presence
bleed deck? Or a Ventrue Vote deck? The individual actions of my opponent's
vampires aren't the focus of the games I play--it is about the large picture.
The tactics are just tactics. If every action my prey takes is a 5th Tradition
(after being Minion Tapped), I am completely unconcerned with whether or not
this is "boring". I am concerned with how the strategic aspect (a vast pool
gain deck) will affect whatever deck I am playing. I build decks to be
consistient and fairly focused. Other than my Rush deck, I am curently playing
a Minion Tap/FOR/Freak Drive/Bleed deck and a Toreador Tap and Bleed deck. They
both are fairly focused and generally take the same actions over and over
again. There are few, if any, surprises in these decks. Sometimes they win, and
sometimes they lose. Just like any other deck.

>>Is this an observation other people can confirm? Does NCL result in more
predictable games?>>

More predictable games? Possibly, in that if I am playing a deck with a focused
strategy and my prey is also playing a focused strategy, I generally know if my
deck will do well or not against my prey's deck, but there are still countless
other interactions to affect the outcome--luck, my predator, his prey, table
talk, politics, whatever. Nothing is ever certain, even with hyper focused
decks.

many times a card can be _used_. If you want to throw multiple copies
of a card in your deck which can only be _used_ once or for which you can
keep only a single copy on the table, go to town. The implications of
that are yours to determine whether they're worthwhile or not.

only keeping a small number of copies of a card in your deck and if you're
influenced by such considerations then luck-of-the-draw is going to make
a difference. But you wouldn't be influenced by it if it made that _much_

much more important than managing to be the guy who played the Giant's Blood
first. That's how they wound up on the restricted list in the first place!
And I don't care that both players _CAN_ play a Time Walk in the same game.
The fact is, you usually don't most of your cards in most games. It's unusual
for either player to draw the card and a huge luck swing if they do. It's
far more unusual for both players to do so. So the "fair" thing you're
talking about is highly unusual.

a bad idea when it was invented, somebody's half-assed compromise to keep
from having to face the music when players couldn't use cards they'd paid
a ton of money for on the open market. And nothing's changed. It's still
a bad idea. Case closed.

really well, there are lots of other things that it can't do at all, and if its
opponent is a well rounded deck and happens to draw the right cards at the
right time, it can shut down the hyper focused deck, just 'cause it happened to

they don't do well overall. People post tournament winning decks all the time
that have weird, all over the place cards and disciplines. Also keep in mind
that certain strategies (vote and S+B) tend to have more room in them for
corner case cards than, say a Rush deck, due to the number of cards needed per
action. A S+B deck needs about 2 cards per action to be sucessful (a stealth
card and a bleed card) where a Rush deck needs like 5 or 6 per action to be
sucessful--thus if you are building an S+B deck, you have more opportunity to
include fringe element cards.

exauhstive list of decks, it is the best list of winning decks we have. I think
you'll find that the decks in question are farily equally split between hyper

I see your point but I feel I have to defend one of my favourite
features of VTES.

I love the unique rule because it prevents the sort of situation you
find in Magic tournaments. Although Magic has some unique cards, they
are very few in number and in general you incur no penalty for the
playing the same cards as other people. In fact, it happens so often
that Magic players often plan ahead for the 'mirror match'
specifically.

The result is that if you turn up to a competitive Magic tournament of
one hundred players, you'll probably find 25 near-identical copies of
each of about three decks and the other 25 a random mixture. The
result is a pretty boring series of games. It happens because anyone
can copy a deck off the internet, turn up and play it without any
penalty. Usually the deck you copy is something that won a tournament
the week before or has been built by a well-respected constructor, so
you know it will be good. Sure, you can take a chance and build
creatively but you don't gain any real advantage for doing so instead
of taking a 'net deck'.

Now, imagine the same picture. A 100 player tournament. 25 people have
turned up playing the deck from that month's Giovanni newsletter, 25
with the deck from the Toreador newsletter and 25 with the deck from
the Gangrel newsletter. The remaining 25 are a random mixture of other
clans.

What happens? Absolute carnage for all those lazy people. Every round,
on average, three out of four tables will have two decks contesting.
Everyone who chose to play a net deck is at a significant disadvantage
and those who exercised some creativity prosper. This is a very good
thing in my opinion and one of the reasons why I now play tournament
Jyhad rather than tournament Magic. ;)

Having said all that, it is possible to play a popular clan and get
around contesting. The last tournament I played, I had eight Ravnos
and four Gangrel in my crypt. I ended up on a table with someone
playing twelve Ravnos (no, really :)) in two games but luckily we'd
chosen fairly different vampires and managed to step around one
another. This was helped by the fact that we had a little negotiation
about transfers in the first couple of turns. :)

All in all, I like the unique rule because if I found myself sitting
down at a table to both prey and be preyed on by identical Ventrue
vote decks regularly, I'd pack this game in pretty quickly.

> - Jason Bell

Cheers,

Phil

Because once-per-game allows players to decide for themselves
how important the effect is and build their deck accordingly.
If I think the Giant's Blood effect is super-key to winning, I
can stick 7 or 17 or 70 of them in my deck in my effort to become
the first one who gets one out. This point means that if the
competition is important, players automatically build a
disadvantage into their decks which compensates for it.

Actually though, I think the real answer to your question is that
Giant's Blood is nearly as important in Jyhad as the cards on the
Magic restricted list. It takes up a valuable master card slot
and only gets built in (in my decks anyway) to large cap decks and
even then is sometimes used at fairly mundane times. (Yippee, I
refilled Democritus when he was down to 7. I'm so happy I could
just shit.)

Granted, it does prevent players from building "Giant's Blood decks"
which revolve around taking advantage of its refill properties. And
if Magic restriction were only used to curb that aspect of certain
cards, I would never have minded. But that's not what it's used for
by and large. Mostly, it's used so a great effect any time anywhere
regardless of whether you build a deck around it can only be lucked
into with one card instead of four. And it can be even be used
multiple times per game if one starts using various Graveyard-digging
cards (principally the also-restricted Regrowth but when you're talking
about things like Time Walk and Ancestral Recall, quite a few other
such cards become worth while). So it doesn't even prevent such things
from being used once per game.

> (the only format with a restricted list) as being terribly large.
> I suspect that from a percentage of cards standpoint, Magic's
> Type I restricted and banned lists are smaller than Jyhad's,
> especially if you include the cards that have been functionally
> changed through errata and later printings.

Actually, if they created a constructed type which allowed players to
use all cards from any editions except those that were banned, as Jyhad
does, the list of cards that should be banned for reasons of being seriously
and unfairly undercosted would make a *HUGE* list! That's one of the
reasons a lot of players give for not creating such a constructed type.
They can't even imagine doing it right, as has been done in Jyhad, because
SO MANY older Magic cards were misdesigned by the standards of the current
designers. This is why Type 1.5 is so biased towards older cards! This is
also why players consistently reject both Types 1.5 and Extended, which has
the same problem on a lesser scale, and stick to Type 2 - then complain that
Magic forces them to spend money on new cards constantly.

As an alternative to banning cards, the DCI could errata the old,
undercosted cards to bring them into line with the current card design
standards. But the DCI has throughout its history rejected the concept of
using errata for this purpose. The stubborn refusal to do either that or
ban any but the absolute worst problem cards was what caused the terrible
player frustration with Jyhad that kept it from ever developing much of a
tournament following when the DCI had control over it. Having bad tournament
rules, IMHO, ultimately affects player satisfaction with a CCG as a whole.
Most players - even non-tournament players - are ultimately unsatisfied with
unbalanced rulesets and look to the tournament rules and rulings to find a
balanced game. When Scott Johnson took over Jyhad and fixed all these
problems that the DCI's flawed philosophies caused, the game has seen a
renaissance which speaks for itself. White Wolf take a game Wizards of the
Coast couldn't make profitable and turn it around? Are they geniuses? I
don't think so. Their only genius was in putting a guy in charge who wasn't
hamstrung by DCI policy.

The DCI would do well to learn from this experience and create a play-
balanced constructed type which allows all card sets. But they'll never
learn.

Legacy of Pander was the popular means to pull it off, yes.

>It seems reasonable to me that a weenie can propose a vote to ban an
>Inner Circle member. What's not reasonable is that the same weenie can
>cast enough votes to make it pass. The problem is weenie voting locks,
>not Banishment abuse.

No, the problem is Banishment abuse. Take a deck with a bunch of
low-caps with pre/PRE, backed by Gideon Fontaine, that already has a
couple Praxis out. The table has mustered enough votes on its own to
keep it in check, such that no vote can pass without the table's
approval OR without a big-PRE modifier.

Gideon calls a KRC, doing 3 to his prey and 1 to himself, with Bribes.
He plays Bewitching Oration on it too, just to make sure. The table
thinks about it, says "let's all gain a pool", and passes the vote.
Cryptic Rider. Banishment on the vamp with the most votes. Cryptic
Rider. Praxis Seizure, and suddenly the weenie deck has vote lock, and
Banishments start landing everywhere. Remember, he's GOT six or more
minions; he can do all this in one turn, though he may have more than
one turn if he happened to hit a voter who was empty.

Sure, it doesn't cost you pool if they were full (rare), but you still
lose the minion for a turn. And if you happen to catch Sheldon at low
blood, that's a -huge- swing in your favor.

I've seen it done, and it's not difficult to set up in your hand; it's
even less difficult to make sure that Gideon can play both a BO and Awe
at the right time to kick off the first "vote" in the Cryptic Rider
chain.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
Orpheus wrote:
>>The same could go with a Malk S&B NCL.>>

Umm, yeah. No. The Malkavians under NCL (i.e. the actual rules) simply aren't
that effective. Under a card limit, the Malkavian's main strategy (stealth and
bleed) is completely unhindered due to the built in redundancy of both bleed
and stealth cards. For instance, under 4CL using only Jyhad cards, a Malk S+B
deck could be built with:

4x Govern the Unaligned
4x Dominate Kine
4x Computer Hacking
4x Conditioning
4x Bonding
4x Threats
4x Lost in Crowds
4x Cloak the Gathering
4x Faceless Night
4x Scouting Mission
4x Mask 2K
4x Veil of Darkness (the rare Obf card that gives everyone +1 stealth...)

Add 12 master cards for a 60 card deck of pure speed S+B. This will be
incredibly effective in a 4CL environment simply because the necessary defenses
(bleed bounce or Rush) are greatly curtailed by the CL, due to a lack of
similar redundancy in necessary cards.

The problem with the Malks under a card limit is that the CL simply doesn't
hinder them at all, because the game was designed to be played with no card
limit, so the fact that there is so much redundancy in Dominate and Obfuscate
cards providing the Malkavians with unlimited ammo in a CL environment wasn't
really an issue. The necessary defenses that made the Malkavians balanced
(bleed bounce and Rush combat), however, are completely hindered by a CL, such
that the Malkavians reign supreme under a CL environment.

Now under the actual rules, the Malkavians aren't any more effective--the
difference between having 4 each of 5 or 6 different stealth cards and having
20 of one stealth card are farily minimal (well, actually, you are better off
with 4 each of 5 than 20 of one...), but the decks that can stand up to them,
namely Rush combat decks and decks with plentiful bleed bounce suddenly become
playable. Thus, the Malkavians fall back in to line.

The Malkavians make effective decks--a S+B deck is strong, sure, but highly
vulnerable to both bleed bounce and Ruch combat. If the prey of a Malk S+B deck
has, say, 12 Deflections in it (which isn't unreasonable for a deck that relies
on bounce as its bleed defense), that Malk deck is in a very bad position--it
goes to bleed, its prey attempts to block, the Malk deck plays a stealth card,
and its prey bounces the bleed down the table. The Malk deck is now bleeding
his grand prey on a regular basis, doing his prey's work for him. The Malk deck
is screwed--he can't oust his prey, and he can't do anything at all, lest he
oust his grand prey, giving his prey 6 more pool and a VP, starting the process
all over again. If a Malk S+B deck is sitting next to a Rush deck, the Malk
deck has zero hope at all--it might not even take a single action the entire
game. When I am playing my Rush deck, if my prey is a Malk S+B deck, I am
totally happy--I torporize every vampire he brings out and oust him quickly. If
my predator is a Malk deck, I generally do the same thing, and get him ousted
rather quickly by my grand predator.

Thus, as a Malk deck can be horribly shut down by two different defenses (bleed
bounce and Rush combat), playing such a deck in competition is gambling that
you won't sit next to such a deck--if you do, you are dead from the get go.

Under the actual rules, Malk S+B is playable and effective, but no more so than
any other viable strategy.

> The conversation was

I'm saying that it's an irrelevant comparison. Once-per-game does
not stop unbalancing one-time-effects. That would have the same
problem that restriction has: an unbalancing effect that goes off
even one time is still an unbalancing effect. It just happens less
often.

> I believe their similarity lies in that problems would
> result if they were allowed in larger quantities.

That's what I strongly disagree with. Most of the cards on the
Magic restricted list have effects that are distinctly unbalancing
with even the play of a single one of them. I do not find that to
be true of Giant's Blood, the primary Jyhad once-per-game card.

> Giant's Blood is just the sort of free-resource boon that Black Lotus is,
> though without the early game-acceleration effect that Black Lotus can

It's that early game-acceleration which is exactly the unbalancing thing.
Keep a fattie out on the table unopposed for four or five turns and you've
won the game - or at least usually you've taken control of it to such an
extent that you can't be stopped. A Black Lotus, which a fairly average
draw around it, can often make that happen. One of the things that makes
such draws so crucial in Magic is the one-card-per-turn resource limit,
which makes some fairly innocent-seeming things actually turn out to be
huge keys. Most of the cards on the restricted list are a lot more
important than a free Master Card fill in Jyhad - especially considering
that a single prince action (5th Tradition) can do the exact same thing.

If you're building a deck without thinking "What happens if I get bled?
What happens if I get bled at stealth?" you really should.

Bleed is the fundamental underlying element of attack, which is entirely
card-less if necessary.

This isn't "building a deck with <S&B Malks> in mind". This is building
a deck that stands a chance against *any* bleed deck.

And a good deck under NL with bleed defence is a perfectly viable
proposition. Wakes (disciplineless, animalism, possibly a side effect
of a Homunculus out of turn deck), bleed reduction (Serpentis,
Chimerstry, Auspex, Greta, independents), bounce (Dominate, Auspex),
intercept (Auspex, Animalism, disciplineless, master cards, Chimerstry,
Necromancy, Obtenebration, 2nd Tradition etc.) are all perfectly viable.

A combat deck doesn't have to plan for stealth and bleed using tactics
different to normal - the Bum's Rushes and Haven Uncovereds (or
whatever) it puts in the deck *are there for expressly that purpose*.
They can rush an annoying voter, an annoying bleeder, an annoying
interceptor or just go forward. It's not special preparation *at all*.
It's building a deck that, due to attacking secondary resources, is
inherently flexible.

A political deck, if it goes via the Ventrue, the Toreador, the
!Toreador, the Lasombra, the !Ventrue, the Tzimisce, the !Tremere and so
on (the people who've been mentioned recently) have access to bleed
bounce. Bleeding is fundamental; you need to have some tactics to cope
with it. (Similarly, what do you do if someone votes? What do you do
if someone rushes your vampires? Are you going to play the odds, the
metagame, or the defence?) A political deck can also use Dramatic
Upheaval or Kindred Restructure to move itself out of the way of any
strategy it doesn't like, very useful. Similarly, Free States Rant is
going to play havoc with such decks. Blood gain is often rare. Forcing
them to spend a turn hunting whilst you suck up pool with Voter
Captivation, and can then do it the following round with probably only
one vote (assuming they hunt for one, you can split three points between
several vampires), is scary. Add Temptation, if you're a Setite deck.

Any deck can try and use speed to outpace the stealth-bleeders - if I
can get to my prey first, going hell for leather, I've got a VP. (The
table wins rules may re-adjust this, of course.) This speed simply
isn't available on a relative scale, under xCL. The Malkavian S&B deck
comes forward at a rate of knots, destroying everything in its path.
Anyone who *isn't* playing Malkavian S&B is slowed down due to the fact
that they can't rely on drawing *anything*.

A deck with a significant bleed element may choose to back-bleed as a
form of defence. "Hey Mr Grand Predator, would you be awfully upset if
I sent this bleed for three at your prey?" Again, such flexible
elements may not be available to an xCL deck, which can't use, say,
multiples of Kindred Spirits. (Or even Night Moves, which is still
excellent.)

Defence against stealth-bleed really isn't hard under NL, once you work
out some reliable, solid tactics. Under xCL, you can work out the
tactics... and then fail entirely to draw them.

Tournament rules that pertain to deck construction and which affect
the game rules directly. Time limits are a provision to move the
tournament along at minimal rate in a shared public facility which may
not be available indefinitely. I think most people have no problem
understanding that it is not a rule intended to affect the outcome of the
game itself, though it sometimes does do so from necessity. Hence, you
apply Time Limits as necessary for your informal game, like when someone's
wife has fetched a softball bat and looks like she'd really like the game
over with at this time of the night. Other rules of that type (e.g.
playtesters, admissibility of sets) are also applied on a local, as-needed
basis. Meaning usually not.

People who want to look at what someone like Peter is saying and take it for
what it's worth shouldn't have too much trouble discerning what "playing
by tournament rules" means in an informal setting. It means simulating the
meaningful rules about deck construction and play and ignoring the ones
whose reasons for existence do not apply to that setting. These little
semantic objections, whether Peter is playing by "house rules" vs. "actual
tournament rules" do not make a very good point, IMO. Call it what you will,
everything he talks about doing is everything I've experienced multiple
other informal play groups doing for the exact same reasons - which is the
point. The use of the pertinent tournament rules insures balance and
allows decks built for them to be transferred from one informal setting
to another seamlessly (as well as directly into tournaments) without
changing the strength of a given deck. The fact that many groups apparently
do this attests to the validity of using these rules. And makes the term
"house rules" inadequate in describing their function.

Fred

Dark Ritual requires a black mana seed and produces only 2 mana of a set

permanent out that forces him to discard and giving yourself unstoppable

and another to keep it on the table. Accelerated mana development, or a
large burst of flexible mana, is something that makes this possible. As
is an extra turn or a burst of extra card draws. Those cards are on the
restricted list for a reason.

Skipping an important point that allows you to understand the "other
way" of thinking is a good way to NEVER make any progress in a discussion,
even if that point could be used as "ammunition" against you.

> The game is actually not *too* poorly balanced under 4CL, which is why

I think this is the most important overlooked point by NCL zealots.
Certain strategies dominate, some are impossible to play, but the game has
it's own goofy "balance" and is still playable. If libraries had to be no
more than 30 cards, or Master cards were banned, or whatever, THEN it's
pretty easy to make the case for "playing by the rules." But simple
evidence that decks that are coincidentally 4CL or nearly 4CL HAVE won
tournaments, even in an NCL environment, shows the format isn't as clearly
broken.

> The problem with 4CL is that it
> strongly favours the suitcase players who have 4 of the rares that
> substitute for the commons that most people use 8 of.

"A" problem more than "The" problem. Much more interesting and telling
is:

> The other
> problem is this: In 4CL, Malks can S&B, Nossies can fight, Ventrue
> and Toreador can vote. That's about it.

First telling point: you CAN make decks that function under xCL. And
play them. And have some sense of balance, and an evolving metagame. And,
most tragically, have fun. Hard to tell people that are having fun "you're
doing it all wrong," especially when their experiences with NCL have been
"not fun."

> In NCL, there are a lot more
> deck types open to you. You can't make a Settite deck at all in 4CL,
> TMK, except perhaps a very weak S&B.

And this IS a problem, and really the biggest problem, and it does shoot
the "creativity" argument in the foot. You are not "forced" to be
"creative" in any way by a 4CL, mostly due to redundant cards with similar
effects. However, an NCL automatically allows for more decks to be created,
because all 4CL decks are a (small) playable subset of NCL. The OPTION of
creativity is limited by a card limit. (Derek addresses this more clearly
in a parallel message.)

Part of the problem with a solution is people trying to "prove" one side
or the other with atypical examples. Yes, you can mow down table after 4CL
table with 4CL S&B, to show them that CL != creative, and CL != balanced.
But a 4CL camper, when opened up to NCL, may immediately make a MT/5th
megabloat deck and crush an uprepared table to "prove the point" about
creativity, and get back to 4CL BEFORE THE METAGAME CAN ADJUST. (Key Point,
could you tell?)
Getting your ass handed to you by a new deck can quickly discourage that
kind of deck from being played, or requires a shift in the metagame to
handle that kind of deck. But I would guess it's easy to mistake the
"problem" as the lack of a card limit: The rules changes, one guy stomped
everyone, no one had fun. What changed? The card limit. Solution?
Reinstall card limit. Fun resumes, all is well.

Okay, how about turning the tables? Why shouldn't the NCLer's try the
4CL and see how it plays?

Well, because we can try it ANY time, just by not putting more than 4 of
any card. 4CL isn't about what you do with YOUR deck, it's about
hamstringing what the OTHER decks do, to limit the kinds of decks you'll be
up against. But we've already played the game long enough under NCL to know
the game is quite balanced. There IS NO "best deck." Quite the opposite.
Furthermore, there's NO correlation between a decks' "winningness" or
"fun factor" and the value of x for the xCL it would fit in. If 4CL is
better than 6CL is better than 8CL (which for most any deck is nearly NCL),
then decks that "break" xCL more and more would win more and more, so if I
have 12 of some card(s) and I'm up against a 4CL deck, I would consistently
win, and consistently have less fun...but that's just not true.

And, most importantly, we're interested (well, most of us, Bakija isn't,
since he's seen it all already) in creative deckbuilding options. The lower
the xCL, the more decks in the "deckbuilding phase space" get knocked out.
You can't mandate creativity, but you could at least allow for it!

*whew!* Okay, there's one more counterarugment to address, but I'll let
someone actually make it before addressing it. =)

one player's position. That is, for the first several turns, their
available mana is one turn ahead of schedule for each mox they drew.
This is often dismissed as minor and in many games it is a minor

this: all different types of cards in a CCG provide a differing
advantage to their user (hopefully it's an advantage, some cards are

level of "power". (The term "power" referring to both the effect and

definition of "power".) There are many, many cards in a game and their
power levels likely can be described as some kind of a statistical
bell-shaped curve. The ones in the middle are so close and squished in
that players' opinions of the cards' power levels will vary more than
the power levels themselves and thus players will eternally disagree
which cards rank where in power. But it's the ones at the top of the
curve that have the potential to really wreck a CCG, assuming they're
far enough away from the rest of the pack. Those are the ones people
need to consider banning - though not necessarily ban.

pack, myself. There did exist such cards in Jyhad, outside the pack too

The thing is, hand strikes can deal ranged damage if they say they do.
If a card said, "make a hand strike. this strike deals ranged
damage", or "your hand strikes are considered to deal ranged damage
until the end of the round", or "deal strength damage, ranged. this
is considered a hand strike" then it would be a hand strike that was
ranged, by explicit card text. These would override the rules text
that says that hand strikes are not ranged, but we already have
provision for that: "where the cards contradict the rules, the cards
take precedence."

The only difference between my hypothetical cards and the combo of
Blood of the Cobra and Scorpion's Touch is that the combo is slightly
ambiguous (very slightly). It results in the equivalent of, "ranged.
make a hand strike." According to the rules,

(6.4.5) When a minion strikes with a hand strike at close range, he
does an amount of damage equal to his strength* to the opposing minion

AND

(6.4.3) Unless the strike is identified as ranged or does "R" damage
(or is a defensive strike such as dodge or combat ends), it is only
effective at close range.

The piece from 6.4.3 does not specifically say that a strike that is
ranged *will* be effective at long range, it simply says that a
non-ranged strike will not be effective at long range. But it
obviously implies that a ranged strike is effective at long range.
The piece from 6.4.5 doesn't say that the hand strike will not be
effective at long range, it seems to imply that it will be effective
only at close range, because it is not a ranged strike.

There is another bit that got quoted saying that a hand strike is a
"non-ranged, non-weapon strike that deals damage based on the minion's
strength." This is meant to imply that a hand strike cannot be
ranged, but forgets the implicit "unless it says it is." A strike
that says it is ranged and says it is a hand strike is a ranged hand
strike, because the cards take precedence.

So essentially, we are left with wondering whether Blood of the Cobra
only allows cards to be *played* as if they were ranged strikes or if
it allows them to take effect as though they were ranged strikes. If
the latter, then it really should work with the Quietus hand strikes.

It was ruled not to do so, which to me constitutes major errata. The
card is not completely useless, but it goes from being a very useful
card to being mostly a waste of time.

The equivalent phrase in English is "to split hairs". Someone who says
that hand strikes only work at close range because of what the rules
say, is splitting hairs. They're trying to impute a meaning where none
was intended. The rules talk mostly about hand strikes in the context
of the default strike that you can make without a card. It's clear that
you can make these at long range because that's what vampires have to do
when they find themselves at long range with no other option - they just
wave their hand. Ordinarily this is not effective in doing damage
because these strikes are not ranged. Blood of the Cobra changes all
that.

It's really quite simple. Hand strikes are strikes made without a
weapon in which your strength determines the amount of damage. It's
mostly a damage thing but also serves as a basis for special effects
like Immortal Grapple. People are confused because most hand strikes,
including the default one, are not ranged. If, by some magic, they do
become ranged then they become effective at range - that's what the term
means. You can't have a ranged strike which is not effective at long
range - that would be an absurd contradiction. A splitting of hairs.

Tsk. I was trying to understand all this better and the natural

I was trying to understand why you need a definition of what constitutes
a hand strike when I'd have thought that it would define itself by use
of the term "hand strike", as on Dagon's Call.

The combat cards seem ok so I started looking at allies. Take
Survivalist, for example. This reads, "Ally with 1 life. 2R damage, 0
bleed...". Ok, supposing this is in combat with someone and wants to
strike them. The rules say, "Each minion chooses his strike. The
strike can be from a combat card, from a weapon the minion possesses or
(the default) a hand strike." The Survivalist will usually have no
weapon or combat card and so it will therefore be doing a hand strike.

We then resolve the strike. The following paragraph tells us how to do
that. We have to assume that the "2R damage" on this ally card relates
to its default strike but that seems reasonable. We therefore see that
the Survivalist will be doing a hand strike for 2 at either close or
long range.

We then have to make sense of 6.4.5. This seems to be a list of special
strike effects and, as none of these bold terms have been used in this
case, we might just pass on. But the first of them indicates that it
relates to the default strike and so it seems reasonable to apply that.
It tells us that when the hand strike is used at close range, you do the
strength as damage and that allies have a default strength of zero. The
Survivalist has no strength in its text so that means it will do no
damage at close range.

So, the conclusion one reaches is that, without a separate weapon or
combat card, the Survivalist will do zero damage at close range, 2
damage at long range and that this is a hand strike.

Or, alternatively, one can conclude that the current card templating and
rules are a mess and that's why people struggle to decipher the game
using 4 year old rulings instead. Who playtests and proof-reads this
stuff - I don't see any credits for this. I trust you will improve the
process for the new Camarilla base set. The third time is the charm.

The end-result of getting this right ought to be that the Survivalist's
built-in strike has the attributes "gun" and "weapon". And that, if he
has some other weapon attached, he could use one or the other but not
both. That, by the way, is the way the Muddled Vampire Hunter should
work too - he clearly comes with his own shotgun. If he has a concealed
Ivory Bow then he might use that instead but would probably not get the
First Strike benefit in that case. Another problem solved.

Andrew
